turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in and have a seat. What brings you in today?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Doctor, I've come out in this awful itchy rash and I can't work out if it was something I ate or the new cream or the antibiotic. I keep panicking that it's something really bad.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): That does sound frightening. Start wherever you like, and tell me how it's been.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The itching kicked off Monday night... sorry, no, it was Tuesday night, so that's three days. I haven't slept properly since, and my head's all over the place.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Three days, then. Where has the rash actually been?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Both arms, and across my tummy as well. I googled rashes and meningitis came up. Is a rash on your stomach a bad sign? Please be honest.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can hear how worried you are. A meningitis rash isn't usually this itchy, but I do want to look properly. Have you felt hot or shivery at all?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think I've had a temperature. I haven't actually checked, though. It fades a bit if I press it. Is that a good thing or not?
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fading when you press it is reassuring. Any swelling of your lips or tongue, or any trouble getting your breath?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. Breathing's been fine and my lips look normal. Should I be setting an alarm to check them in the night?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll give you clear warning signs before you go, I promise. You mentioned food, a cream, and an antibiotic — can you walk me through those?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, Monday night I had prawns, a stir-fry. My sister was there banging on about her biotin tablets for her hair, which is her thing, not mine. Could prawns wait a whole day and then do this?
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sometimes a food reaction shows up later, yes, though often it's quicker. Did you feel ill while you were eating, or only afterwards?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I was completely fine at the table. The itch didn't start till Tuesday night. So is that too slow for the prawns? I can't stop going round in circles.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not too slow to rule it out, and not quick enough to prove it either. Tell me about the new cream.

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): It's Epimax, the ointment. I got it for my dry elbows. I can't remember the day I started — sometime last week, maybe Thursday, I genuinely don't know. If I only put it on my elbows, why is my stomach itchy? That doesn't add up, does it?

[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): A contact rash usually stays where the cream has been, so the tummy makes a straightforward contact reaction less likely. Did any of it get on your hands or anywhere else?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the elbows and a bit on my shins. Not my tummy, I'm sure. Should I bin it? It cost me a tenner and I don't want to throw money away if it's not the cause.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd stop using it for now, until we've a better idea. Money aside, it's the safer move. What about the antibiotic — what were you given, and what for?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Flucloxacillin, for my finger. It's infected, all red round the nail. They told me two hundred and fifty milligrams... no, wait, I've got the box, it's five hundred milligrams, four times a day.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five hundred milligrams four times a day. When did you start it, and are you still taking the doses?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I started Saturday, so five days, and yes I'm still taking it. My mum rang the receptionist this morning and more or less answered for me. She got the flucloxacillin right, but she said the rash has been a fortnight and that I'm allergic to penicillin, and that part isn't right.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm glad you've put that straight. So you yourself are not allergic to penicillin?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, she's mixing me up with my brother, who came out in a rash with penicillin when he was little. I've had penicillin loads of times and I was fine, so I am not allergic to it. Is flucloxacillin even a penicillin, though? That's the bit that's scaring me.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is a penicillin-type antibiotic, yes. With this rash I'd like you to stop the flucloxacillin from today. If the finger flares we can rethink.

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Stop it completely, even the ones for tonight? What if the finger gets worse and I end up on a drip? And if I tolerated penicillin before, why would this one give me a rash? I don't get it.

[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): People sometimes react to one penicillin and not another, and this rash may not be the drug at all. I can't separate the prawns, the cream, and the flucloxacillin today. Stopping it is just the safe step while you're itchy.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): All right. There was a prescription for prednisolone as well, thirty milligrams, but I never took a single tablet. I was too scared of steroids. And I used to take cetirizine, but I stopped it in May — no, March, when the hay fever packed up.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you never started the prednisolone, we can leave that out. The cetirizine you stopped in March — do you remember the dose?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligrams, once a day. I'm definitely not on it now. Would an antihistamine even work if we don't know the cause, or could it hide something important?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): It should ease the itch whichever of those three it is, and it won't hide a serious infection. Any other allergies — medicines, foods, plasters, anything?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of. Only my mum's penicillin story, and that's wrong. If this is an allergy, is it permanent? Am I never eating prawns again? I really like prawns.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't stamp a lifelong allergy on you from one muddled episode. Let me see the rash. Sleeves up, and I'll look at your tummy too.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): It's got worse since this morning, I know it has. Can you see it spreading? Please say if you can.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can see a red, bumpy rash over both forearms and across the lower abdomen. It blanches when I press it. There are no blisters, and your lips and tongue look normal.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Blanching means it isn't meningitis, yes? You're sure? My heart's been racing all morning from the worry. I can feel it now.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not seeing a meningococcal rash. Your temperature is thirty-six point eight and your pulse is eighty-eight, which suits someone anxious rather than someone very unwell. Any vomiting, diarrhoea, or tummy pain along with this?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Tummy's fine, no sickness. It's just the itch, and it's worse at night. I was up till two. Is that the rash or just me panicking?

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Itch often gets worse at night, so that fits the rash rather than pure panic. Putting it together, this looks like an urticarial rash, hives, but I can't say if it's the prawns, the Epimax, or the flucloxacillin. That's a working impression, not a firm diagnosis.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't actually know. What do we do, then? Do I need blood tests? I read about patch testing — is that a thing for me? And can I please have something so I can sleep tonight?

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): No blood tests today. We could refer you for patch testing, but I wouldn't do that straight away. Let's try an antihistamine first, and if the rash hasn't settled in two weeks, then I'd arrange the patch test.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So the patch test only happens if it's still there? What do they actually do? Does it hurt? And please don't give me cetirizine again — I don't want the one I stopped. Is that a ridiculous thing to ask?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not ridiculous at all. I'll use loratadine instead, ten milligrams once a day, by mouth, for the itch. Patch testing is patches stuck on your back for a couple of days — more of a nuisance than painful. We might do that only if this hasn't cleared in a fortnight.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Once a day, even if I'm clawing at myself at midnight? Morning or evening? And am I stopping the Epimax as well as the flucloxacillin, or just one of them?

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take it in the morning. Stop the Epimax and stop the flucloxacillin. Leave prawns alone until this has gone, and we can talk about them later. If your lips swell, your tongue feels tight, or you're breathless, call 999.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): 999, got it. What about the finger, though? It's still a bit red. If I stop the antibiotic am I going to end up in hospital? I work in a nursery and I can't just disappear.

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the finger gets more painful, starts discharging, or you develop a fever, come back the same day or ring the surgery. I wouldn't keep you off nursery work for this rash alone, as long as you feel well in yourself.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): OK. If the loratadine hasn't worked by the weekend, do I come straight back or do I have to wait the whole two weeks? Sorry, I know I'm asking a lot.

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't apologise, these are sensible questions. If you're worse, or you get swelling or breathlessness, don't wait. If you're well and it's simply still itchy, give it the two weeks, then book back and we'll arrange patch testing if it's needed.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Book back if it's not better in two weeks. And the loratadine — you'll put it on a prescription, won't you? I don't have to buy it over the counter?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll put it on a prescription now. Loratadine ten milligrams, once daily. Was there anything else you wanted to ask?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Just one thing. You're not quietly worried it's something awful and softening it for me? I'd rather you were blunt.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll be blunt. I think this is hives with an unclear trigger, not meningitis and not an emergency today. Stop those two new things, start the loratadine, and we'll see you if it hasn't settled in two weeks.

spec.situation: Itchy rash after 'something I ate or the new cream or the antibiotic'; patient unsure which; a family member says the same happened with penicillin in childhood, patient denies. No firm diagnosis; patch test or antihistamine.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

bad.reason: Patient was asked about diarrhoea but did not explicitly mention it.

Blisters absent is supported, but body site forearms and lower abdomen was not specified for blisters.
